screens.title: Deep Dive into ERC-20
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will explore ERC-20, the standard interface that defines fungible tokens on Ethereum. We will unpack the mandatory functions and events every ERC-20 token implements, and you will learn how token amounts are represented with decimals so you can avoid common unit mistakes. You will see how direct transfers differ from delegated transfers, and how the approve, allowance, and transferFrom trio enables third parties like exchanges to move tokens on a user’s behalf. We’ll examine a frequent pitfall — the allowance race condition — and practical mitigations such as resetting allowances or using safe increase/decrease helpers. You will also learn security practices like following Checks-Effects-Interactions and verifying contract addresses before approving tokens. Finally, a hands-on mock token and terminal-style deployment demo will let you try balanceOf, transfer, approve, allowance, and transferFrom on a local test network. By the end you should be confident reading ERC-20 interfaces, calculating token base units correctly, and interacting safely with tokens in DApps and scripts.

screens.title: What is ERC-20?
screens.narratorSegment: ERC-20 is the technical specification that defines a minimal interface for fungible tokens on Ethereum. At its heart it prescribes a set of functions and events so that wallets, exchanges, and smart contracts can interact with any compliant token in a predictable way. This mutual agreement is why tokens interoperable across wallets and DeFi exist. The key mandatory items include metadata functions like name, symbol, decimals, and totalSupply; balance and transfer functions such as balanceOf and transfer; and the allowance suite: approve, allowance, and transferFrom, along with two events: Transfer and Approval. A practical example: a wallet reads name and symbol to label the token, uses decimals to render human amounts, calls balanceOf to show a user’s balance, and listens for Transfer events to update histories without scanning all blocks. A common misconception is that ERC-20 prescribes behavior beyond its surface interface; it does not mandate supply models or permissioning. That means tokens can implement minting, burning, or unusual accounting internally, but as long as they expose the standard functions and events, external systems can work with them. As a takeaway, treat ERC-20 as an interoperability contract: it gives you expectations about how to query and move fungible units safely.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › What is ERC-20?
Definition

ERC-20 is a standard interface for fungible tokens that specifies a small set of functions and two events. It enables wallets, exchanges, and contracts to handle tokens in a predictable way.

Key functions
  • Metadata: name(), symbol(), decimals(), totalSupply()
  • Balances & transfer: balanceOf(), transfer()
  • Allowance flow: approve(), allowance(), transferFrom()
Key Takeaway

ERC-20’s minimal interface creates broad compatibility: if a token implements the functions and emits the events, external tools can work with it.

Analogy & Example
Think of ERC-20 as a bank’s API specification for accounts and transfers. Any bank that exposes the same endpoints can be integrated into the same accounting dashboard. For example, a wallet reads decimals to display human amounts and listens for Transfer events to update transaction history without heavy state reads.
Event
Transfer
Emitted when tokens move, letting off-chain services track transfers efficiently.
Event
Approval
Emitted when an allowance is set, enabling delegated transfer workflows.
Common misconception: ERC-20 does not dictate how tokens are minted or burned, or how balances are internally accounted for. It only guarantees an interface that external systems can call and rely on.

screens.title: Token Metadata and Decimals
screens.narratorSegment: Token metadata functions are small but critical. name and symbol provide human-readable labels for wallets and UIs. decimals defines how many fractional digits a token supports and determines how numeric values are represented inside the contract, which only works with integers. totalSupply returns the total number of base units minted. Understanding decimals is especially important because it converts human amounts into base units used in contract calls. For example, a token with decimals equal to 18 uses 10**18 base units per whole token. If decimals is 6, then one token equals 1,000,000 base units. A common error is passing the human number directly to transfer without scaling: sending 1 when decimals is 18 moves one base unit, not one whole token. A concrete example from the chapter: if decimals() returns 6 and you want to send 1.5 tokens, you must call transfer with 1_500_000 as the uint256 amount. Another practical point: contracts may override decimals; don't assume 18. Always read decimals() and perform the multiplication in your scripts. A quick check is to display both raw base units and the human-scaled amount in the UI so users can confirm they are sending the intended value.

keyIdea.title: Decimals matter
keyIdea.text: Always read decimals() and convert human token amounts to contract base units before calling transfer or approve to avoid sending the wrong quantity.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Token Metadata and Decimals
Metadata functions
  • name(): human-readable token name, e.g., MyToken.
  • symbol(): ticker-like abbreviation, e.g., MTK.
  • decimals(): number of decimal places; used to convert between human amounts and base units.
  • totalSupply(): total tokens in base units.
Practical rule: always call decimals() in your client or script and compute amount * (10 ** decimals) before sending transactions. Present both base units and human values in your UI so users can verify amounts.
Concrete example
If decimals() returns 6 and you want to transfer 1.5 tokens, compute: 1.5 * 10^6 = 1_500_000. Call transfer(recipient, 1500000). Sending the number 1 would transfer one base unit, not one whole token. Always scale in your scripts.
Common mistake
Passing human amounts without scaling leads to transfers that are orders of magnitude off. This is a frequent source of lost tokens in demos and scripts.

screens.title: Direct Transfers and Events
screens.narratorSegment: Direct transfers are the simplest way tokens move. The owner of tokens signs a transaction that calls transfer(recipient, amount). The token contract first checks the sender has sufficient balance, updates internal balances, and then emits a Transfer event to signal the movement. balanceOf(address) is a read-only function that returns the current token balance in base units. A typical flow: a user script calls balanceOf to show a balance, then creates a transaction that calls transfer with the scaled amount. Upon transaction confirmation, off-chain services and wallets that listen for Transfer events update histories and balances without re-querying every state slot. An important principle to apply in contract design and interaction is Checks-Effects-Interactions: check conditions, apply state changes (effects), and then interact with external contracts. While plain ERC-20 transfers usually stay internal, more complex token functions that call external contracts can introduce reentrancy if they perform external calls before finishing state updates. A concrete example: transfer from Alice to Bob reduces Alice’s balance and increases Bob’s, then emits Transfer(Alice, Bob, value). A common misconception is that Transfer events are authoritative; events are off-chain signals and may be omitted or malformed in a broken implementation, so always rely on contract state for security-critical checks.

keyIdea.title: Direct transfer rule
keyIdea.text: A transfer checks balance, updates balances, and emits Transfer. Events help off-chain systems, but contract state is the source of truth.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Direct Transfers and Events
Transfer flow
  1. Caller constructs transfer(recipient, amount) with amount in base units.
  2. Contract checks caller balance >= amount.
  3. Contract updates state: decrease sender, increase recipient.
  4. Contract emits Transfer(from, to, value) event.
Off-chain systems subscribe to Transfer events to reflect token movements in UIs and analytics without scanning full state every block.
Example
Alice calls transfer(Bob, 2000000000000000000) on a token with 18 decimals to send 2 tokens. The contract reduces Alice's balance by 2 * 10^18 and increases Bob's by the same amount, then emits Transfer(Alice, Bob, 2000000000000000000).
Misconception
Events are helpful signals but not authoritative. For a security-sensitive check, always read contract state with balanceOf.

screens.title: Delegated Transfers: approve, allowance, transferFrom
screens.narratorSegment: Delegated transfers enable a third party, called a spender, to move tokens from an owner’s account once the owner grants permission. The owner calls approve(spender, amount) to set an allowance; this emits an Approval(owner, spender, value) event. The allowance(owner, spender) function returns the currently approved amount. Later, the spender calls transferFrom(sender, recipient, amount). The token contract checks that sender has sufficient balance and that allowance(sender, spender) is at least amount. If checks pass, balances change and the allowance is reduced by amount. This pattern supports use cases such as an exchange moving funds to execute a trade, or a staking contract deducting fees. A concrete example: Alice approves a DEX contract for 500 tokens (scaled by decimals). The DEX then calls transferFrom(Alice, Pool, tradeAmount) to settle trades, and the allowance is decremented accordingly. A common misconception is believing allowance changes automatically without explicit approve calls; only approve updates allowance. Also note that allowances are stored per owner-spender pair. For secure integrations, log and surface allowance values to users and ensure your UI multiplies approved numbers by decimals for clarity. Finally, remember that transferFrom will fail if allowance or balance is too low, so front-end checks help improve UX but do not replace on-chain validation.

keyIdea.title: Delegated transfer
keyIdea.text: approve grants permission, allowance returns permitted amount, and transferFrom consumes allowance while moving tokens from the owner to a recipient.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Delegated Transfers
Three-step pattern
  1. Owner calls approve(spender, amount) → Approval event emitted.
  2. Query allowance(owner, spender) to confirm the approved amount.
  3. Spender calls transferFrom(owner, recipient, amount); allowance and balances update.
Keep UI state in sync with allowance values so users understand what they have permitted. Only transferFrom reduces the allowance; approvals are explicit actions by the token holder.
Example scenario
Alice calls approve(DEX, 500 * 10**decimals()). The DEX later calls transferFrom(Alice, Recipient, tradeAmount). The contract checks Alice’s balance and allowance, reduces Alice’s balance and the allowance by tradeAmount, and emits Transfer and potentially Approval updates.

screens.title: Allowance Race Condition & Mitigations
screens.narratorSegment: The allowance race condition happens when a token owner changes an existing non-zero allowance by calling approve with a new value while a malicious spender observes the pending transaction. If the spender notices the original approve is still valid, they can call transferFrom and drain the prior allowance before the owner’s new approval takes effect. The classic pattern to avoid this is to first call approve(spender, 0) to clear the existing allowance, then call approve(spender, newAmount). This two-step sequence narrows the window where the spender can act on the old allowance. A practical alternative is to use libraries like OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 which provide safeIncreaseAllowance and safeDecreaseAllowance helpers; these functions require knowledge of the current allowance and update it atomically, preventing blind replacement. Concrete example: owner had allowance 100, wants to set to 50. Instead of approve(50), call approve(0) and after it confirms, call approve(50). Misconception: some developers think one approval transaction replaces another instantly — on-chain ordering and mempool timing make pending transactions observable. Treat allowances as state that can be consumed before your new approval finalizes. From a UX perspective, surface the reset pattern and consider recommending small approvals or pull-based spending models where possible.

keyIdea.text: Reset allowance to zero before setting a new value, or use safe increase/decrease helpers to avoid front-run spending of prior allowances.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Allowance Race Condition & Mitigations
The problem
If you replace a non-zero allowance directly, a spender can observe the pending approve and call transferFrom using the old allowance before your new approval lands. This can lead to unintended extra spending.
Safe pattern
  • Call approve(spender, 0) and wait for confirmation.
  • Call approve(spender, newAmount) to set the desired allowance.
Helpers & UX
Libraries like OpenZeppelin provide safeIncreaseAllowance and safeDecreaseAllowance which adjust allowance relative to the current value and reduce front-run risk. From the user interface side, warn users about approving large amounts and suggest resetting allowances when updating permissions.
Example
Owner reduces allowance 100 → 50. Use approve(spender,0) then approve(spender,50) instead of a single approve(spender,50).

screens.title: MockERC20.sol Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: We’ll walk through the provided MockERC20 contract used for testing and demos. It imports OpenZeppelin’s ERC20 base and, in the constructor, mints an initial supply to the deployer scaled by decimals. The contract includes a public mint function for tests and overrides decimals to return 18 — a common testing choice. This mock is simple yet representative: because it inherits from a well-tested ERC20 base, it exposes name, symbol, decimals, totalSupply, balanceOf, transfer, approve, allowance, transferFrom, and emits the expected Transfer and Approval events. When reading the code, pay attention to the _mint call in the constructor: initialSupply_ * (10 ** decimals()) mints base units for the initial supply. That multiplication is the same scaling you will perform in scripts. The mint function is public here only for convenience in tests — in production, unguarded mint functions are a serious risk. A misconception to avoid: test contracts often include helper functions or relaxed access that should never be copied verbatim into production systems. Use this mock locally to practice transfers and allowances, but when deploying to a live network, prefer audited, production-hardened contracts without public minting unless intended.

keyIdea.title: Mock contract purpose
keyIdea.text: The mock token provides a safe local environment to practice transfers, allowance updates, and unit conversions without risking real funds.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › MockERC20.sol Walkthrough
Starter code
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

import "@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/ERC20.sol";

contract MockERC20 is ERC20 {
  constructor(string memory name_, string memory symbol_, uint256 initialSupply_) ERC20(name_, symbol_) {
    _mint(msg.sender, initialSupply_ * (10 ** decimals())); // Mint initial supply to deployer
  }

  function mint(address to, uint256 amount) public {
    _mint(to, amount);
  }

  function decimals() public view virtual override returns (uint8) {
    return 18; // Standard 18 decimals
  }
}
Note the scaling in the constructor: initialSupply_ * (10 ** decimals()). That mirrors what you must do in scripts. Also note the public mint helper — useful in tests but unsafe in production without access controls.
What to try
  • Deploy locally with a name, symbol, and initial supply and check balances.
  • Call mint from another account to see balance changes and events.
  • Practice approve and transferFrom flows between test accounts.
Safety note

Do not copy test helpers like a public mint into production contracts unless guarded by proper access control.

screens.title: How a DEX Uses Approve & transferFrom
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the system-level architecture helps you reason about who calls which function. In a common DEX flow, three actors are involved: the token owner (user), the spender (DEX contract), and a recipient (liquidity pool, counterparty, or the DEX itself). First, the user calls approve(DEX, amount), granting the DEX contract permission to spend a specific amount. The DEX contract, when executing a trade or a swap, calls transferFrom(user, recipient, tradeAmount) to move tokens. The token contract enforces that the user has enough balance and that the DEX has sufficient allowance for that user. Architecturally, keep in mind the separation of concerns: the token contract manages balances and allowances; the DEX implements trade logic and calls transferFrom as needed. From a security viewpoint, the DEX should design its flows so that it cannot be tricked into transferring more than intended — using pull patterns and explicit recipient addresses helps. A practical example: a user approves 500 tokens to a DEX; the DEX might call transferFrom to move 100 tokens to a pool for a trade, then later move another 200 for settlement. Always design the DApp to display current allowance and remaining allowance to users, and recommend resetting approvals when they are no longer required. This architectural clarity prevents surprises and helps with auditing interactions between token and application contracts.

screens.title: Allowance Lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: Think of allowance as state that evolves over time. The lifecycle begins when an owner calls approve(spender, amount), creating or replacing an allowance entry and emitting Approval. At any later time the spender can call transferFrom(owner, recipient, amount), which performs checks and reduces the stored allowance by amount. If the owner wants to change permissions, they call approve again; to mitigate race conditions they should first approve(spender, 0) and then approve(spender, newAmount). Each transferFrom call produces a Transfer event and typically results in an allowance decrease, which observers can track. A common operational flow in a DApp: owner approves, DApp executes multiple transferFrom calls for each action up to the allowance, and the owner monitors allowance via allowance(owner, spender) to see remaining permitted funds. Keep in mind allowance changes only occur through explicit approve calls or when transferFrom consumes allowance. A useful practice is to display a timeline in the UI showing the original approve, subsequent transferFrom operations that decremented the allowance, and any approve changes, so users can audit how their permission was consumed. This visibility reduces surprises and aids troubleshooting when balances or allowances appear unexpected.

Owner grants allowance. Approval event emitted.

Spender moves tokens, allowance reduced by the amount.

Owner may reset to zero then set new allowance to avoid races.

screens.title: Security Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: When working with ERC-20 tokens, be mindful of contract-level security even though the token functions appear simple. Reentrancy is a general risk when token interactions involve external calls. While transfers that only update internal balances are usually safe, token operations that invoke external contracts or are called from untrusted code can expose reentrancy paths. The recommended defense is to follow Checks-Effects-Interactions: validate conditions first, then update internal state, and only after that interact with external contracts. Another essential practice is verifying contract addresses before approving tokens. Malicious DApps may trick users into approving their contract, allowing them to drain tokens. Always confirm the spender contract address and scope approvals tightly. Regarding allowances, prefer the reset-to-zero pattern or safeIncreaseAllowance and safeDecreaseAllowance helpers to avoid front-run race conditions discussed earlier. Use audited libraries like OpenZeppelin when possible, as they encode common protections. Finally, do not rely solely on events: read and assert contract state when making security decisions. A practical checklist: verify spender address, minimize allowance, reset before change, use safe helpers, follow checks-effects-interactions, and rely on audited implementations for production deployments.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Hands-on: Deploy and Test MockERC20
Terminal sequence (illustrative)
# Deploy with Hardhat (example)
npx hardhat run scripts/deployMock.js --network localhost

# After deploy, check balances in a script using ethers
const decimals = await token.decimals();
const amount = ethers.utils.parseUnits('1.5', decimals); // scales to base units
await token.transfer(recipient, amount);

# Approve and transferFrom
await token.connect(owner).approve(spender.address, ethers.utils.parseUnits('500', decimals));
console.log('allowance before', (await token.allowance(owner.address, spender.address)).toString());
await token.connect(spender).transferFrom(owner.address, recipient.address, ethers.utils.parseUnits('100', decimals));
console.log('allowance after', (await token.allowance(owner.address, spender.address)).toString());
These commands show the critical steps: scale with decimals, approve, then transferFrom while logging allowance to observe the lifecycle.

Question: If decimals() returns 6 and you want to send 1.5 tokens, what integer do you pass to transfer()? Answer: 1_500_000. Practice this conversion in your script to avoid unit errors.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will explore ERC-20, the standard interface that defines fungible tokens on Ethereum. We will unpack the mandatory functions and events every ERC-20 token implements, and you will learn how token amounts are represented with decimals so you can avoid common unit mistakes. You will see how direct transfers differ from delegated transfers, and how the approve, allowance, and transferFrom trio enables third parties like exchanges to move tokens on a user’s behalf. We’ll examine a frequent pitfall — the allowance race condition — and practical mitigations such as resetting allowances or using safe increase/decrease helpers. You will also learn security practices like following Checks-Effects-Interactions and verifying contract addresses before approving tokens. Finally, a hands-on mock token and terminal-style deployment demo will let you try balanceOf, transfer, approve, allowance, and transferFrom on a local test network. By the end you should be confident reading ERC-20 interfaces, calculating token base units correctly, and interacting safely with tokens in DApps and scripts.

By the end of this lesson you will identify each mandatory ERC-20 function and event and explain their purpose in practical terms. You will be able to calculate token base units using the decimals parameter and avoid common unit mistakes when transferring tokens. You will understand the difference between direct transfers initiated by a holder and delegated transfers performed by an approved spender, and you will be able to describe the approve, allowance, and transferFrom sequence that enables delegated spending. Finally, you will recognize allowance-related race conditions and name mitigation patterns such as resetting allowance to zero or using safe increase/decrease helpers. These skills matter when you write contracts that interact with tokens, when you approve DApps, or when you build user interfaces that display token values accurately. A quick example: if a token uses 6 decimals, you will convert 1.5 tokens to 1_500_000 base units before calling transfer. Practicing these objectives with a mock token makes the concepts concrete and reduces costly mistakes in live deployments.

This lesson is equally about technique and safety. You will demonstrate reading and calling ERC-20 functions from a script or the Remix console, including name, symbol, decimals, totalSupply, balanceOf, and allowance. You will write a small script that converts human-readable token amounts into base units using decimals before calling transfer, avoiding a frequent user mistake. You will simulate a delegated transfer: approve an allowance from an owner account, then call transferFrom from a spender account and confirm allowance reduction and balance changes. For safety, you will observe and reason about the allowance race condition, and practice mitigations such as calling approve with zero before changing values or using increase/decrease helpers that require a known current allowance. Understanding these patterns prevents accidental over-approval and reduces the risk of token loss when interacting with unfamiliar contracts. These objectives prepare you to build UIs, backend services, or smart contracts that interact safely with ERC-20 tokens.

ERC-20 is the technical specification that defines a minimal interface for fungible tokens on Ethereum. At its heart it prescribes a set of functions and events so that wallets, exchanges, and smart contracts can interact with any compliant token in a predictable way. This mutual agreement is why tokens interoperable across wallets and DeFi exist. The key mandatory items include metadata functions like name, symbol, decimals, and totalSupply; balance and transfer functions such as balanceOf and transfer; and the allowance suite: approve, allowance, and transferFrom, along with two events: Transfer and Approval. A practical example: a wallet reads name and symbol to label the token, uses decimals to render human amounts, calls balanceOf to show a user’s balance, and listens for Transfer events to update histories without scanning all blocks. A common misconception is that ERC-20 prescribes behavior beyond its surface interface; it does not mandate supply models or permissioning. That means tokens can implement minting, burning, or unusual accounting internally, but as long as they expose the standard functions and events, external systems can work with them. As a takeaway, treat ERC-20 as an interoperability contract: it gives you expectations about how to query and move fungible units safely.

Token metadata functions are small but critical. name and symbol provide human-readable labels for wallets and UIs. decimals defines how many fractional digits a token supports and determines how numeric values are represented inside the contract, which only works with integers. totalSupply returns the total number of base units minted. Understanding decimals is especially important because it converts human amounts into base units used in contract calls. For example, a token with decimals equal to 18 uses 10**18 base units per whole token. If decimals is 6, then one token equals 1,000,000 base units. A common error is passing the human number directly to transfer without scaling: sending 1 when decimals is 18 moves one base unit, not one whole token. A concrete example from the chapter: if decimals() returns 6 and you want to send 1.5 tokens, you must call transfer with 1_500_000 as the uint256 amount. Another practical point: contracts may override decimals; don't assume 18. Always read decimals() and perform the multiplication in your scripts. A quick check is to display both raw base units and the human-scaled amount in the UI so users can confirm they are sending the intended value.

Direct transfers are the simplest way tokens move. The owner of tokens signs a transaction that calls transfer(recipient, amount). The token contract first checks the sender has sufficient balance, updates internal balances, and then emits a Transfer event to signal the movement. balanceOf(address) is a read-only function that returns the current token balance in base units. A typical flow: a user script calls balanceOf to show a balance, then creates a transaction that calls transfer with the scaled amount. Upon transaction confirmation, off-chain services and wallets that listen for Transfer events update histories and balances without re-querying every state slot. An important principle to apply in contract design and interaction is Checks-Effects-Interactions: check conditions, apply state changes (effects), and then interact with external contracts. While plain ERC-20 transfers usually stay internal, more complex token functions that call external contracts can introduce reentrancy if they perform external calls before finishing state updates. A concrete example: transfer from Alice to Bob reduces Alice’s balance and increases Bob’s, then emits Transfer(Alice, Bob, value). A common misconception is that Transfer events are authoritative; events are off-chain signals and may be omitted or malformed in a broken implementation, so always rely on contract state for security-critical checks.

Delegated transfers enable a third party, called a spender, to move tokens from an owner’s account once the owner grants permission. The owner calls approve(spender, amount) to set an allowance; this emits an Approval(owner, spender, value) event. The allowance(owner, spender) function returns the currently approved amount. Later, the spender calls transferFrom(sender, recipient, amount). The token contract checks that sender has sufficient balance and that allowance(sender, spender) is at least amount. If checks pass, balances change and the allowance is reduced by amount. This pattern supports use cases such as an exchange moving funds to execute a trade, or a staking contract deducting fees. A concrete example: Alice approves a DEX contract for 500 tokens (scaled by decimals). The DEX then calls transferFrom(Alice, Pool, tradeAmount) to settle trades, and the allowance is decremented accordingly. A common misconception is believing allowance changes automatically without explicit approve calls; only approve updates allowance. Also note that allowances are stored per owner-spender pair. For secure integrations, log and surface allowance values to users and ensure your UI multiplies approved numbers by decimals for clarity. Finally, remember that transferFrom will fail if allowance or balance is too low, so front-end checks help improve UX but do not replace on-chain validation.

The allowance race condition happens when a token owner changes an existing non-zero allowance by calling approve with a new value while a malicious spender observes the pending transaction. If the spender notices the original approve is still valid, they can call transferFrom and drain the prior allowance before the owner’s new approval takes effect. The classic pattern to avoid this is to first call approve(spender, 0) to clear the existing allowance, then call approve(spender, newAmount). This two-step sequence narrows the window where the spender can act on the old allowance. A practical alternative is to use libraries like OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 which provide safeIncreaseAllowance and safeDecreaseAllowance helpers; these functions require knowledge of the current allowance and update it atomically, preventing blind replacement. Concrete example: owner had allowance 100, wants to set to 50. Instead of approve(50), call approve(0) and after it confirms, call approve(50). Misconception: some developers think one approval transaction replaces another instantly — on-chain ordering and mempool timing make pending transactions observable. Treat allowances as state that can be consumed before your new approval finalizes. From a UX perspective, surface the reset pattern and consider recommending small approvals or pull-based spending models where possible.

We’ll walk through the provided MockERC20 contract used for testing and demos. It imports OpenZeppelin’s ERC20 base and, in the constructor, mints an initial supply to the deployer scaled by decimals.
